Name: reasoning_length_contagion
Title: Length Contagion: How the Previous Problem Anchors How Long a Reasoning Model Thinks About the Next One
Short Hypothesis: A reasoning model's thinking budget for the current problem is contaminated by the reasoning length of immediately preceding problems in its context: after a long/hard predecessor it overthinks an easy current problem, and after a short/easy predecessor it underthinks a hard one. This length contagion is causally carried by a length-budget representation in the prompt-boundary residual stream that persists from the previous problem, is dissociable from the current problem's true difficulty, and steering it restores difficulty-appropriate length.
Related Work: Prior work shows reasoning length is planned pre-generation for a SINGLE problem: 'On Reasoning Strength Planning' (2025) finds a pre-allocated directional vector whose magnitude sets token count from question activations; 'When More is Less' (2025) and 'Critical Thinking' (2025) characterize an optimal length tied to a problem's own difficulty; ThinkEdit/Efficiency Steering/S3-CoT identify and steer a length direction. All treat each problem in isolation and assume length is a function of that problem's difficulty. Separately, 'Extrapolation by Association' (2025) shows length-generalization can transfer across jointly-trained tasks via shared attention heads, but studies training-time capability transfer, not inference-time contamination of budget by neighboring items. No prior work asks whether the length budget for problem N is anchored by problems N-1, N-2 in the same context, nor identifies a carried-over budget representation as the cause. Our contribution is a new inference-time phenomenon (length contagion / anchoring across problems), its dissociation from the current problem's difficulty, and a causal account via a persistent length-budget representation.
Abstract: Reasoning language models allocate a thinking budget that is assumed to track the difficulty of the problem they are currently solving. We challenge this assumption at the level of context: real deployments feed problems in sequence (multi-turn chats, batched evaluation, agentic loops), and we ask whether the reasoning length of preceding problems contaminates the budget spent on the current one. We hypothesize length contagion: after a long, hard predecessor a model overthinks an easy current problem, and after a short, easy predecessor it underthinks a hard current problem, holding the current problem fixed. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we construct paired contexts that place the SAME target problem after predecessors of controlled difficulty/length and measure the shift in target reasoning length and accuracy. We test whether contagion is dissociable from true difficulty via a mixed-effects decomposition of length variance into predecessor vs. target factors. Mechanistically, we test whether a length-budget representation read at the target's prompt boundary carries over from the predecessor: a linear probe should predict target length partly from predecessor-induced state, activation patching of the prompt-boundary state from a short-predecessor context into a long-predecessor context should transfer the budget, and steering along the length-budget direction should cancel contagion and restore difficulty-appropriate length. We quantify the efficiency and accuracy cost of contagion (overthinking-after-hard, underthinking-after-easy) and offer a training-free debiasing intervention. Our work reveals a context-level anchoring failure in reasoning allocation and its causal locus.
Experiments:
1) Establish contagion (behavioral): Build a controlled matrix of two-problem (and multi-problem) contexts. For each TARGET problem (drawn from GSM8K/MATH500/AIME/GPQA spanning easy-to-hard) create variants that place it after a PREDECESSOR of low difficulty/short reasoning vs high difficulty/long reasoning (predecessors drawn from the same benchmarks; predecessor reasoning shown in-context). Keep the target text identical across variants. Measure target reasoning-token count and accuracy per variant. Metric: within-target change in target length as a function of predecessor difficulty/length; report effect size and whether accuracy shifts (over/underthinking). Control for prompt position/context length using a neutral filler-predecessor of matched token length (isolates predecessor DIFFICULTY/LENGTH from raw context length).
2) Dissociation from true difficulty: Fit a mixed-effects model of target reasoning length with random effect for target identity (its intrinsic difficulty) and fixed effects for predecessor difficulty and predecessor length. Hypothesis: a significant predecessor effect after accounting for target identity. Report variance attributable to predecessor vs target. Compare to a difficulty probe trained on the target alone to show predecessor carry-over adds predictive power beyond target difficulty.
3) Location - carried-over length-budget probe: At the target's prompt boundary (last token before any target reasoning token), extract residual-stream activations. Train a linear probe to predict target reasoning length. Test whether, for identical targets, the probe's prediction shifts with predecessor difficulty (i.e., the boundary state has absorbed the predecessor's budget). Layer sweep to localize. Compare against 'On Reasoning Strength Planning'-style single-problem length direction to test whether contagion rides the SAME direction.
4) Causal Intervention - patching: Patch the prompt-boundary residual state (candidate layers) from a short-predecessor context into the matched long-predecessor context (same target) and vice versa; measure whether target length transfers toward the donor context. Report sign, dose (patch strength / layer subset), and specificity (matched-random-direction patch and off-target accuracy controls).
5) Causal Intervention - debiasing steering: Derive a length-budget steering direction (difference-of-means between short- and long-predecessor boundary states, or the probe weight). At the target boundary, steer to cancel the predecessor-induced offset and restore a difficulty-appropriate budget. Metrics: reduction in predecessor-driven length variance, accuracy recovery on hard-after-easy (underthinking) items, token savings on easy-after-hard (overthinking) items; compare to no intervention and to fixed truncation/budget-forcing baselines.
6) Efficiency/accuracy cost quantification: Estimate, over a realistic mixed-difficulty problem stream, how many tokens are wasted (overthinking-after-hard) and how much accuracy is lost (underthinking-after-easy) due to contagion, versus an oracle per-problem budget. Report Pareto accuracy-vs-tokens.
7) Generalization: transfer probe/steering across datasets and model scales without retraining; test multi-predecessor decay (does contagion fade with distance / number of intervening problems?) and whether contagion appears in genuine multi-turn chat and batched-evaluation formats.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Predecessor effects could be driven purely by context length/position rather than by the predecessor's difficulty; the matched-length neutral-filler control and the mixed-effects decomposition are designed to isolate this, and a null after controls would be an informative negative result. Contagion may be small or model-specific (strongly instruction/RL-tuned models may reset budget per problem); we report effect sizes across scales/families. The length-budget probe may conflate carried-over state with re-derived target difficulty; the identical-target-across-predecessors design and patching experiment address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and harm coherence; we use matched-random-direction controls and report sample validity. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters, limiting to models with explicit thinking segments. Debiasing gains may not exceed simple per-problem budget-forcing, but the phenomenon and its causal locus are the primary contribution. Multi-turn chat formats may introduce confounds (the model treating predecessors as user intent) that we characterize but cannot fully eliminate.
